Photo by Gregory Cooper, NLR 93997 12 https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acsnano.4c15809 13 https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemmater.5c00455 30 | Advanced Computing Annual Report 2025 Advanced Computing Annual Report 2025 | 31 Fast Neuromorphic Computing Hardware for Next Gen AI Neuromorphic computing, which mimics the structure and function of the human brain, offers a potential pathway for implementing energy-efficient AI. A key challenge in designing ion- based neuromorphic hardware is understanding how atomic-scale interactions in materials affect conductivity, switching behavior, and long-term stability—properties that directly influence the speed and energy efficiency of neuromorphic devices. Neuromorphic architectures rely on massive numbers of low-power, densely interconnected memory elements, such as electrochemical random-access memories (ECRAMs), whose conductance is tuned by ions moving from an ion reservoir, across the electrolyte, and into and out of the channel. In this project, researchers investigate ECRAM architectures that incorporate atomically thin, two-dimensional channel materials, whose conductivity is highly sensitive to the local ionic environment at the electrolyte/channel interface. Even small improvements in ion conductivity or charge transport at these interfaces can translate into significant reductions in total energy consumption. By modeling the atomic and electronic structures of potential new materials, researchers aim to better understand these interactions and identify material combinations that will maximize conductivity response while minimizing energy losses across ECRAM devices used in neuromorphic computing. Funded by the Semiconductor Research Consortium’s Joint University Microelectronics Program 2.0 and using Kestrel for extensive first-principles calculations, researchers provided new insights into the suitability of materials for these devices. Findings from this work, published in MRS Advances,14 show how specific chemical configurations and atomic interactions alter the electronic and structural stability of promising device materials. This detailed understanding is critical, because stable interfaces and predictable electronic behavior are key to optimal operation in neuromorphic devices and circuits. By illuminating how atomic-level structure governs macroscopic performance, the team helps inform the design of next-generation materials that can support faster, more efficient neuromorphic computing hardware—advancing the development of AI systems that operate with dramatically lower energy requirements. < Close-up of RAM modules installed on a Kestrel CPU compute node.
